title: Robin Sloan - Writing with the machine: GPT-2 and text generation
speaker: Robin Sloan
summary: Novelist Robin Sloan presents the craft of generating fiction with GPT-2 through a case study: about a thousand mailed fantasy quest stories whose parameters came from a $0.99 reader survey and a procedurally generated map with generated place names. He fine-tuned GPT-2 on high fantasy novels and drove it with a sequence of short, partly authored prompts that each request a specific number of sentences, letting generated text accumulate as world state. He discards any output that trips his filters, argues the result outpaces template-based text, and recommends pinning generated text to a framework like a map, using GPT-2 as a description engine, steering with sharp prompt turns, and hidden prompts. His justification is that the language is beautiful and surprising and flexibly guidable.

insights.claim: Sloan generated and mailed about a thousand GPT-2 fantasy quest stories, each parameterized by a reader survey and tied to a custom procedurally generated map.
insights.detail: The fiction was that an academy of wizards simulates possible quests against a Dark Lord on their 'mage frames', and readers define one quest's parameters for $0.99. Letters looked like crusty mainframe reports and were mailed via the Lob API; he suggests a play-by-mail game is waiting to be built with it. Every quest ends in defeat.
insights.quote: I wanted to send people fantasy stories quest tales generated by a machine learning system

insights.claim: Sloan's quest survey offered preset options alongside free-text fields so that readers who didn't feel creative could still parameterize a quest.
insights.detail: Questions covered who starts and leads the quest, what they seek (a sword, chalice, book, severed head) and what they encounter (an elk, a dragon, a melancholy giant). The resulting CSV of player inputs (a theologian, a basketball star, a swarm of ticks) was itself a delight.
insights.quote: I didn't want anybody to be stalked by the sense that they like didn't know how to even parameterize a quest

insights.claim: Sloan used generated place names from each reader's map as inputs to the text generator, so the map and the story share names and the story feels set in a real place.
insights.detail: He calls the place names the glue: you hold the map in one hand and the story in the other. The story can say 'on the road towards Ningbag' and the reader can trace the route on the map.
insights.quote: these place names became the key the glue that you hold your map in one hand and your story in the other

insights.claim: Sloan drove GPT-2 with a simple prompt format that requests a specific number of sentences per prompt, a key expressive control versus letting it generate endlessly.
insights.detail: Each prompt mixes his authored text ('began their quest in') with reader inputs and ends with a sentence count. Sometimes one sentence was enough; elsewhere two or three let a little scene build. He didn't want to seed it and receive pages of dense text, but to guide it at every turn.
insights.quote: I'm telling the system how many sentences I want this turns out to be a key expressive control

insights.claim: Sloan chained prompts without clearing context, so earlier generated sentences accumulate into a world state that shapes later output.
insights.detail: By the last prompt the context is roughly half his prompts and half the model's own text. In a sample quest, the 'land of the dead' introduced paragraphs earlier recurred later, which he says no prior system he used could do: they produced lovely sentences but lost the thread.
insights.quote: by the time we get to the last prompt here it's actually built up a state of the world

insights.claim: Sloan fine-tuned the internet-pretrained GPT-2 on a small corpus of high fantasy novels for about a week, overwriting its sensibility with high fantasy while keeping its grasp of English.
insights.detail: He calls fine-tuning crucial. The pre-training remains in its grammar and sentence construction, but it learned to guess the next word in a fantasy-style sentence.
insights.quote: I didn't fine-tuned that on a much smaller group of high fantasy novels that I gathered from various sources trained in on that for about a week

insights.claim: Sloan warns it is never responsible to pipe raw GPT-2 output straight to players or readers, since it can produce anything from mildly gross to horrifying content.
insights.detail: Even fantasy novels contain weird material. His mailed quests are raw output from his system but heavily filtered, not raw GPT-2 output.
insights.quote: it's never responsible to pipe the output from one of these systems certainly GPT two straight out into the world into a player's face

insights.claim: Because GPT-2 can generate text cheaply and endlessly, Sloan used a simple veto: any block that tripped a filter was discarded and regenerated rather than edited.
insights.detail: He found throwing output away and asking for something new easier and cleaner than trying to re-edit or stitch pieces of it.
insights.quote: I adopted a really simple Vito system if it put spit out a block of tax that triggered any one of my many many many filters

insights.claim: Sloan argues language-model output outpaces even nested text templates because templates' seams show after a few reads, turning the pattern rather than the words into the unit of enjoyment.
insights.detail: Read one template output and it's interesting; read five and you sense the pattern and think 'oh it's one of those'. If you care about the language, you lose something when readers see the Rubik's Cube beneath. GPT-2 is also a template, but one as large as the library or the language.
insights.quote: I think you always see the seams I think you read one and it's interesting I think you read five and you start to sense the pattern

insights.claim: Sloan recommends pinning generated text to a systematic framework like a map, dramatis personae, family tree, spell list or bestiary, which acts as a rhythm section while the language riffs.
insights.detail: Text offloads work to the reader's brain, and that effect multiplies when it is anchored to a structure. He imagines words appearing in places on a browser map with Indiana Jones-style arrows. The map keeps the beat (port, mountain, city, road) while GPT-2 talks about elk with wings like the night sky.
insights.quote: I think that that effect is multiplied when that text gets pinned to some kind of framework so in my case it was a map

insights.claim: Sloan steers GPT-2 with 'sharp turns', short authored prompt fragments like 'a city known for' or 'the Dark Lord truly' that inject motion or drama and channel the output.
insights.detail: Without such prompts, simply stating something and asking for continuation gives more variable results that let the machine decide everything. He calls these fragments the most fully authored part of the project and says these tiny twists made a huge difference.
insights.quote: I found that these super simple little twists just really made a huge difference and kind of channeling the creative potential of the system

insights.claim: Sloan suggests using GPT-2 primarily as a description engine, since language models are happiest describing things; descriptions can be generated offline, filtered and stored, or generated live.
insights.detail: Running 'the village of Firepuddle was known for' many times yields varied, surprising descriptions like 'prodigious haystacks' that readers fill in with meaning. Even when outputs are stringently filtered to fit a template, he believes they keep diversity a hand-written template would lack.
insights.quote: probably the first thing I would say is this can be your description engine

insights.claim: Sloan's subtlest trick is a hidden prompt: guidance fed to the model but replaced (e.g. with nothing) in the shown output, whispering what kind of scene comes next.
insights.detail: His format uses an extra pipe so the prompt 'the world was quiet' is given to the model but not displayed, producing stillness like 'only the water and birds sang'. He says the technique applies beyond GPT-2, to other neural nets and probably Markov chains.
insights.quote: I'm giving it a prompt and asking it for a completion and I'm saying keep that prompt to yourself

insights.claim: Sloan says a generator must earn its place by producing beautiful, surprising, guidable language, echoing roguelikes' healthy suspicion of the shiny new thing.
insights.detail: Interest in a technical trick alone is not enough reason to use it in a work. Roguelikes show an old or forgotten technology can fire the imagination better than a new one. He also values that generated text leaves gaps for readers to fill.
insights.quote: roguelikes are built on this judicious Ness the sense that like the right technology even if it's an old one
